chapter_theme: Gandharvadattai's spell shows Civakan to his grieving brother and carries Nandattan to Emamapuram, where Vijayan and Vasundari find a stranger in Civakan's likeness and the brothers meet.

cast.role: the Vidyadhara king's daughter, Civakan's wife, who stays behind in Rajamapuram
the great deity that carries the sleeping Nandattan to Emamapuram
a prince of Emamapuram who learns the bow from Civakan and calls him brother-in-law
a woman of the Emamapuram palace who finds the stranger at the bow-practice ground

1701.reading: Pushing aside with her lute-playing hand the soft cushion stuffed with silk-cotton from pods red as torn flesh and green as squirrels, the garlanded woman lies long lost in thought.
1701.event: Gandharvadattai leaves her cushion and broods on the absent Civakan.
1701.nuance: The woman is not named; the yāḻ hand (யாழ்கை) and the next verses' visit of Civakan's younger brother identify her as Gandharvadattai, the vina player.

1702.reading: Thinking of her lord, she sighs hot breaths, the beauty of her red mouth dulls and the sword-eyed woman wastes.

1703.reading: While she sits wondering when her young breasts will press the garlanded chest of her lord again, Civakan's younger brother comes to her.
1703.event: Nandattan comes to Gandharvadattai as she longs for Civakan.

1704.reading: He stands five bow-lengths away and bows at her feet; she looks at him in wonder and bids Kama without bow or arrow come and sit, and the spear-bearer bows again three times.
1704.event: Nandattan bows to Gandharvadattai from a distance and she bids him sit.
1704.nuance: The distance kept (ஐவில் அகலம்) and the repeated bow mark the deference of a younger brother before his elder brother's wife.

1705.reading: He looks neither at her moon face, nor her breasts, nor her girdled hips, but only at the anklet on her small foot, and asks where his lord is.
1705.event: Nandattan, eyes on her anklet, asks Gandharvadattai where Civakan is.

1706.reading: Nandattan reasons that if the meritorious one were dead she would have put off garland, bangles and pearls and taken either the path of penance or the long fire, for he knows of no wife who bears ornaments when her husband is gone.

claims.claim: a wife whose husband dies puts off her ornaments and either keeps a vow of penance or enters the fire

1706.nuance: The norm is not urged on anyone; it is used as evidence: her ornaments prove to him that his brother lives. The two courses are set side by side with ஒன்றோ ... ஒன்றோ, neither ranked above the other.

1707.reading: As the prince withers like a wishing tree caught by fire and stands in the burning of his love for his brother, the bee-hung woman begins to speak.
1707.event: Nandattan grieves for his brother and Gandharvadattai begins to answer.

1708.reading: She answers that the prince with the spear does not think of them; he has gone to the marriages fate brings him and sits enjoying them, and asks why she, who knows it, should waste away.
1708.nuance: The sense of மதிமுகம் அறியும் நாமே in line 4 is unclear: it may be 'we who know his ways' or refer to a moon-faced mirror of her lore; the bitterness about விதிமுக மணங்கள், marriages set by fate, is a wife's sulk, not a doctrine.

1709.reading: She says that if he grants what she asks he will see his brother; the youth agrees to be her servant for seven births, and she recites a fine spell and strokes a moon-like face, which lights up the far place he thinks of as if it were near.
1709.event: Nandattan promises Gandharvadattai lifelong service, and her spell shows him the distant place.
1709.nuance: What she strokes (மதிமுகம்) is doubtful: her own face, or a mirror-like surface on which the vision appears; the verse does not say what she asked in return.

1710.reading: On a golden couch's flower bed he sees first his brother, crowned with a wishing-tree garland, dressing a woman's dark hair; he smiles, joins his hands and stands with his body cooled.
1710.event: In the vision Nandattan sees Civakan dressing his new wife's hair, and worships.
1710.nuance: The woman whose hair Civakan dresses is not named; the ilampakam's story makes her Kanakamalai.

1711.reading: When the honey-voiced woman withdraws the spell, he, bewildered at heart since what he saw was only a seeming, bows and begs her grace that he may reach his lord's feet.
1711.event: Gandharvadattai ends the vision and Nandattan begs her to send him to Civakan.
1711.nuance: பொய்ய தன்மையின் (line 3) is read as the unreality of the image; it could also be a mark of his not lying.

1712.reading: She orders garlands, sandal paste, a gold sword and a dagger, hair perfume and fine ornaments to be brought to the place.
1712.event: Gandharvadattai has gifts and weapons brought for Nandattan's journey.
1712.nuance: The division பதிக்கட் டம்மென is doubtful; it is read here as an order to bring the things to the place.

1713.reading: The radiant youth puts on the many ornaments as she bids and goes in, and the garlanded woman then recites her spell.
1713.event: Nandattan adorns himself and Gandharvadattai begins the spell.

1714.reading: She smears the place with sandal, hangs garlands of chosen flowers, raises agil smoke, and withdraws with her young women.
1714.event: Gandharvadattai prepares the chamber with rites and leaves.

1715.reading: When the youth, like Kama's younger brother, has lain down on the smoke-scented couch, a great deity sets him down in Emamapuram, they say.
1715.event: A great deity carries the sleeping Nandattan to Emamapuram.
1715.nuance: The verse names the deity's act and not Gandharvadattai's; the spell of 1713 is what binds them.

1716.reading: Shining like a wishing tree in flower with jewels and gold, the youth rises from sleep as the sun climbs the great hill.
1716.event: Nandattan wakes at dawn in the new place.

1717.reading: As the hero sent by the red-lipped woman sits there, Vijayan, bow in hand, sees him and comes near.
1717.event: Vijayan finds the stranger and approaches him.

1718.reading: Asked who he is, the stranger with a god-fragrant body gives no answer, and Vijayan goes quietly back and tells it to his brother-in-law.
1718.event: Nandattan does not answer Vijayan, who goes to tell Civakan.
1718.nuance: மைத்துனன் makes Civakan Vijayan's brother-in-law, through the marriage seen in 1710.

1719.reading: Vijayan reports that Vasundari, carrying sandal paste, flowers, water in a gold pot, agil, pearls and a lamp to worship at the bow-practice ground, came and told him what she saw.
1719.event: Vasundari goes to worship at the archery ground and reports a stranger.
1719.nuance: 1718 says Vijayan told 'this' to Civakan and 1722 closes with என்றான், so 1719 to 1722 are read as his speech, with Vasundari's words quoted inside it; the verse could also be the narrator's.

1720.reading: Vasundari tells how she wondered why their lord had left his agil couch to lie on the bare ground, went to tell her companion, and found him there with the princess, and she warns that it may be a magic.
1720.event: Vasundari finds the double of Civakan on the ground while Civakan is with his wife.
1720.nuance: Her அடிகள் is the stranger she took for Civakan; the likeness of the brothers drives the scene.

1721.reading: Vijayan says he went to see as she told him, and found a lion-like youth with sword and shield beside him whose youth, beauty, bearing and form are, in a word, stamped with Civakan's likeness.
1721.event: Vijayan goes to look at the stranger.
1721.nuance: சொல்லின் நிற்பொறி ஒற்றிக் கொண்டான் is read as 'he has taken your seal', that is, he looks like you; the image is not certain.

1722.reading: He describes the stranger's long arms, red eyes, dark curled hair, necklace, gold-rubbed skin, hanging earrings and kuvalai garland, and says he does not know who the handsome man is.

1723.reading: Hearing the words gladly, Civakan knows that the youth is Nandattan, come with the message of the peacock-like woman, and goes without delay to where he is, they say.
1723.event: Civakan recognises his brother from the description and goes to him.

1724.reading: Like the sun breaking from a black cloud to walk on the sea, Civakan comes with shining face, and his younger brother, like Arjuna seeing Dharma after long, joins his hands and falls worshipping at his feet.
1724.event: Nandattan falls at Civakan's feet as the brothers meet.
1724.nuance: The simile of தனஞ்சயன் and தருமன் sets the brothers in the Pandava pattern of a younger brother's devotion to the eldest.

links.note: In 351 the widowed Vijayai strips her pearls, bangles and rings; here Nandattan reasons from Gandharvadattai's unremoved ornaments that Civakan lives.
links.teaches: The stripping of ornaments that the epic first showed as a widow's grief becomes, read backwards, a sign a kinsman can read, so jewels on a wife are public evidence of a living husband.

links.note: Thirikadugam lists a husbandless woman's adornment among things unfit; Nandattan argues from the same norm that a wife still adorned has a living husband.
links.teaches: The ethical list states the rule as unfitness, while the epic turns that rule into a piece of inference, showing the norm was strong enough to serve as proof of a fact.

gains.a: the Cintamani's argument gains a stated norm outside the story, so Nandattan's reasoning rests on a known rule and not on a guess
gains.b: the bare rule gains a scene in which someone actually relies on it to learn whether a man is dead

links.note: Puram 246's queen rejects the widow's austerities and chooses the pyre; Nandattan names penance and the fire as two equal courses for a widow.
links.teaches: Where the Sangam queen ranks the fire above the hard widow's life, the Jain epic's speaker leaves the two as alternatives, so the pair shows the choice the queen made was one of two recognised paths.

gains.a: Nandattan's passing phrase gains the weight of a real choice argued for in the Sangam queen's own voice
gains.b: the queen's refusal gains a later witness that the austere path she scorned stayed a full alternative to the fire

links.note: The Kural praises the manhood that does not look at another's wife; Nandattan, who must meet and speak to his brother's wife, keeps his eyes on her anklet.
links.teaches: The couplet forbids the look outright, and the scene shows how the rule is kept when a man must face and address the woman: the gaze goes to her feet, where looking becomes reverence.

gains.a: Nandattan's lowered eyes gain a named virtue, so the verse reads as conduct and not only courtesy
gains.b: the couplet gains the case it does not cover, a kinsman's obliged meeting, and the bodily form its restraint then takes

links.note: In 1147 Gandharvadattai's recited spells bring armed powers to free Civakan; here her spell shows Civakan far away and then sends his brother to him.
links.teaches: Her vinjai, first a weapon of rescue, becomes a means of sight and passage over distance, so the Vidyadhara wife is the household's power to reach Civakan wherever he goes.

links.note: The patikam says the younger brother, desolate as a star that has lost the moon, came to join Civakan at a woman's bidding; here Civakan sees that Nandattan has come with the peacock-like woman's word.
links.teaches: The patikam's 'by a woman's command' is shown to mean Gandharvadattai's spell and bargain, so the summary's single phrase hides a whole scene of grief, vision and magical travel.

new_concepts.gloss: the vidya: the spell-lore of the Vidyadharas, recited to summon powers, show distant things or carry a person
new_concepts.label_source: 1709 has விஞ்சை; also declared in ch050

source_issues: Most verses were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the build (FLAG repaired); word division inside joined lines is often doubtful.
1708 line 2 ends with a stray full stop (உள்ளான்.).
